findings.claim: the Last Supper (Jesus shares bread and wine with his disciples, saying “This is my body... this is my blood of the new covenant”)
findings.truth: Luke 22:19-20, the passage the spec names (Luke 22-24), reads “This is my body given for you” and “This cup is the new covenant in my blood”. ‘This is my blood of the covenant’ is Matthew 26:28 / Mark 14:24, not Luke.

findings.claim: He said the bread was his body and the wine was his blood of the new covenant.
findings.truth: Same Luke misquote as F1. In Luke the cup is the new covenant in his blood; the bread is his body given for them.

findings.claim: “Describe Christian beliefs about the Incarnation.” typed as “3 marks — Describe”
findings.truth: In this spec ‘Describe’ is a 4-mark command word and it is not used on this paper. The 3-mark part (a) uses ‘Outline three’.
findings.evidence: spec Appendix 3 command-word table (State 3, Outline 3, Describe 4, Explain 4 or 5, Evaluate 12); Paper 2 structure (a) 3 / (b) 4 / (c) 5 / (d) 12

findings.claim: “Discuss this statement.” / “12 marks — Discuss a Statement”, repeated in the exam tip as “a 12-mark Discuss question”
findings.truth: The 12-mark command word on this paper is ‘Evaluate’. ‘Discuss’ is another board’s wording and is not in this spec’s command-word table.

findings.claim: The most likely comparison in the exam is Islam or Catholic Christianity.
findings.truth: For the starred point 1.6 the comparison must be with another religion practised in Great Britain: Buddhism, Hinduism, Islam, Judaism or Sikhism. Catholic Christianity is a Christian tradition, so it cannot serve as the compare-and-contrast religion.
findings.evidence: spec Area of Study 2B overview, comparison requirement for 1.6* and 2.1*

findings.claim: “Describe what the 39 Articles of Religion teach about life after death.” typed as “3 marks — Describe”
“Discuss this statement.” / “12 marks — Discuss a Statement”, and “On 12-mark Discuss questions” in the exam tip
findings.truth: Same command-word error as F4. The 12-mark part is ‘Evaluate’.

findings.claim: “Describe how Pentecostal Christians worship differently from Anglican Christians.” typed as “3 marks — Describe”
“Discuss this statement.” / “12 marks — Discuss a Statement”, and “a 12-mark Discuss question” in the exam tip
Christian Aid … working in over 40 countries (repeated in the key fact, the glossary entry and a flashcard answer)
findings.truth: Christian Aid works with partners in about 24 countries. ‘Over 40’ overstates the reach of the one development agency this spec names. Corrected to ‘more than 20 countries’, which stays true as the figure moves.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Christian Aid (‘across 24 countries’); Christian Aid’s own site gives no country total

findings.claim: “tens of thousands of young people … visit Taizé” in the main text, but “hundreds of thousands of young Christians annually” in the collapsible and “tens of thousands” again in a flashcard
findings.truth: Taizé receives over 100,000 young people a year. The two figures in the lesson contradict each other and one overstates.

findings.claim: “Describe what Christians celebrate during Holy Week.” typed as “3 marks — Describe”
“Discuss this statement.” / “12 marks — Discuss a Statement”, and “For the 12-mark Discuss on mission” in the exam tip

The unit quotes scripture from three different English versions: L1 and L4 use NRSV/ESV wording (“the Word became flesh and lived among us”, “This is my beloved Son”, “proclaim the good news to the whole creation”) while L2 and L3 use NIV (Psalm 103:8, Psalm 119:71, 2 Corinthians 5:10, Matthew 6:6-7).
findings.truth: Every quotation is verbatim in a mainstream version and every reference is correct, so nothing here costs a mark. The choice is whether the programme forces one version (NIV) across the unit, which would mean rewriting five quotations in L1 and L4 and re-narrating them, or accepts the present mix. Recommendation: accept the mix and leave the text alone.
findings.evidence: BibleGateway NIVUK; NRSV wording checked against the quoted phrases
findings.ruling: Leave: translation mix accepted; all quotations verbatim.

findings.claim: Holy Week: “The final week of Lent, beginning on Palm Sunday … and ending on Easter Sunday”
findings.truth: Easter Sunday is not part of Lent; Lent ends on Holy Saturday. The phrasing is loose but it is how most GCSE textbooks put it, and the lesson’s own flashcard already says ‘the final week before Easter’. Not worth an edit.
findings.evidence: internal comparison with the L4 flashcard; standard liturgical calendar

findings.claim: “These two sites are Edexcel-specific pilgrimage sites not commonly found in other GCSE specifications”; “Iona is significant as the birthplace of Scottish Christianity”
findings.truth: Iona is also a named pilgrimage example in AQA’s Christianity practices, so ‘Edexcel-specific’ overstates. ‘Birthplace of Scottish Christianity’ is the traditional claim for Iona but Whithorn is earlier. Neither claim is examined, so no edit.
findings.evidence: spec 2.4 (Jerusalem, Iona, Taize, Walsingham); general knowledge of the AQA Christianity practices content

findings.claim: 12-mark mark schemes use the band names “Mastering (10-12) / Secure (7-9) / Developing (4-6) / Emerging (1-3)” in all four lessons
findings.truth: The mark ranges are right and the names are not a board’s wording, but they are not the house band vocabulary (Top band / Upper-mid band / Mid band / Lower-mid band / Low band). This belongs to the band-ladder workstream, not to a fact-check edit.

summary: Doctrine, creeds, the 39 Articles (XXII and XXV), denominational attribution, the named pilgrimage sites and every knowledge-check answer key are correct; the damage is concentrated in the exam framing, where all four lessons use another board's 'Discuss' command word for the 12-mark part and carry a 'Describe' question at 3 marks that this spec does not have. One real scripture error: the Last Supper words in L1 are Matthew/Mark wording attributed to Luke 22-24.
